concepts.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search: HNSW and IVF
concepts.description: Brute-force exact k-nearest-neighbor search is correct but scales linearly with the number of stored vectors, which stops being fast enough well before a collection reaches production scale. Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms like IVF and HNSW trade a small, tunable amount of accuracy for order-of-magnitude speedups by exploiting the same clustered structure in embedding spaces that makes similarity search meaningful.
learningObjectives: Explain why brute-force exact kNN search is O(n) per query in the number of stored vectors, and why that fails to scale to large production collections.
Explain why classical exact spatial index structures degrade toward brute-force performance in high dimensions, motivating approximate methods.
Describe, at a conceptual level, how IVF narrows a search to a small number of clusters instead of scanning the entire collection.
Describe, at a conceptual level, how HNSW performs layered greedy graph traversal to find near neighbors quickly.
Explain what 'approximate' means in ANN search: that recall below 100% is an accepted, tunable tradeoff for speed, not a defect.

sections.heading: Brute Force Is Correct but Doesn't Scale
sections.body:
The previous concept ended on the brute-force kNN algorithm: compare the query against every stored vector and keep the best k. That algorithm is *correct*: given enough time, it always finds the true nearest neighbors, with no approximation. The problem is scale. Its cost is O(n * d) per query, where n is the number of stored vectors and d is their dimensionality, because there's no way to know how similar the query is to a vector without looking at that vector's coordinates.

A linear-in-n cost feels fine in development and becomes untenable in production. A demo with 10,000 documents does a brute-force scan in a few milliseconds, imperceptibly. A real knowledge base for retrieval-augmented generation, or a product catalog for semantic search, can easily reach tens or hundreds of millions of vectors. At that scale, a full scan per query, multiplied across every concurrent user, becomes the dominant cost and latency bottleneck of the system, and throwing more CPU at the inner loop buys only a constant-factor improvement against a cost that still grows linearly with your data. (Brute force with SIMD or on GPUs handles millions of vectors comfortably, so where the crossover falls depends on your latency budget and hardware.) If your product grows, your brute-force latency grows with it, with no ceiling.

sections.heading: Why Classical Exact Indexes Don't Save You Either
sections.body:
A natural next idea, if you've worked with spatial data, is an exact indexing structure like a **KD-tree** or **ball tree**. These hierarchically partition space so that, for low-dimensional data (2D map coordinates, 3D point clouds), you can prune huge swaths of the search space without computing a distance to most points, giving sub-linear query time while still finding the *exact* nearest neighbor.

The unfortunate news is that this approach degrades badly as dimensionality grows, for reasons tied to the curse of dimensionality covered earlier in this subject. The pruning strategy relies on being able to say 'this whole branch is definitely farther than what I've already found, so I can skip it,' and that confident pruning gets harder to justify as dimensions increase, because in high dimensions the boundary of almost any spatial partition passes close to almost every query point. Past a certain dimensionality, these trees end up visiting nearly every node anyway to be sure they haven't missed anything, so you pay for maintaining the tree and get none of the pruning benefit. A common rule of thumb is that trees stop helping somewhere around a couple dozen dimensions, and for embeddings with hundreds of dimensions, exact tree-based indexes are not a reliable win over brute force. This is the gap approximate methods fill: they give up the guarantee of finding the *exact* top-k, in exchange for algorithms that scale far better and, because embedding spaces are clustered rather than randomly scattered (as covered earlier), still find something extremely close to the true answer almost all the time.

sections.heading: IVF: Cluster First, Then Search Only What's Relevant
sections.body:
**IVF (Inverted File Index)** is one of the more intuitive ANN approaches, and it works in two phases. Offline, as an indexing step, it clusters the stored vectors into `nlist` groups, typically with a k-means-style algorithm, and records each cluster's centroid (its geometric center). Every stored vector is associated with exactly one cluster: whichever centroid it's closest to.

At query time, IVF compares the query against the (far fewer) *centroids* first, picks the `nprobe` closest, and only then scans the vectors in those `nprobe` clusters. With `nlist = 1000` and `nprobe = 8`, 'compare against every stored vector' becomes 'compare against 1000 centroids, then against roughly 8/1000 of the vectors,' a dramatic reduction for a large collection:

```python
def brute_force_ops(n):
    return n   # one distance computation per stored vector

def ivf_ops(n, nlist, nprobe):
    vectors_per_cluster = n / nlist
    return nlist + nprobe * vectors_per_cluster   # centroids, then only the probed clusters

n = 1_000_000
print(brute_force_ops(n))                      # 1000000
print(int(ivf_ops(n, nlist=1000, nprobe=8)))   # 9000: over 100x fewer comparisons
```

This is where the 'approximate' part comes from: clustering partitions space with hard boundaries, but real data doesn't respect them. A stored vector can be very close to the query yet assigned to a *different* cluster than the query's nearest centroid, because it fell just on the other side of a boundary during clustering. If that cluster isn't among the `nprobe` probed, IVF never sees the vector and it's missing from the results, even though brute force would have found it. Raising `nprobe` buys back that lost recall at the cost of scanning more vectors, and so more latency. `nprobe` is the most important dial for trading speed against accuracy in an IVF index, and the next concept covers how to tune it.

sections.heading: HNSW: A Graph of Shortcuts
sections.body:
**HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)** takes a different approach: instead of clustering, it builds a **graph** where each stored vector is a node connected to a handful of nearby nodes. The graph is built in **layers**. The bottom layer contains every vector, densely connected to its close neighbors, like local streets for fine-grained navigation once you're in the right neighborhood. Each layer above holds a smaller, randomly selected subset of vectors with longer-range connections, like a highway system that covers large distances in few hops. The top layer may contain only a handful of nodes, sparsely connected across the whole space.

Searching works by starting at a fixed entry point in the top (sparsest) layer and greedily walking: at each step, look at the current node's neighbors in this layer, and move to whichever one is closest to the query; repeat until no neighbor is closer than the current node, which gives a locally good point for this layer. At that point, drop down to the next layer (which has that same node, plus many more, more densely connected), and repeat the same greedy walk there. By the bottom layer you're already close to the true nearest neighbors and need only a small amount of local searching to collect the top-k candidates (the bottom-layer search keeps a candidate list of size `ef_search` rather than following a single path).

Think of getting to a distant city: you don't search every side street in the country, you take the highway for most of the distance and switch to local streets once you're near. HNSW's layers build that idea into a graph, and it's why HNSW search typically examines only a tiny fraction of the stored vectors, usually orders of magnitude fewer than n, to find near-exact nearest neighbors. Two parameters control the graph's shape: `M`, the maximum number of connections each node keeps per layer (larger M means a denser, more accurate, but more memory-hungry and slower-to-build graph), and `ef_search`, the size of the candidate list kept during the greedy search (larger means the search considers more candidates before settling, trading latency for recall). Both are covered in the next concept.

sections.heading: Approximate Is a Dial, Not a Compromise Forced on You
sections.body:
'Approximate' can sound like a euphemism for 'worse,' so reframe it. Brute-force search offers no levers: you get the exact answer at one cost. ANN algorithms hand you a dial (`nprobe` for IVF, `ef_search` for HNSW) that lets *you* decide, for your product, where to sit between 'slightly less than 100% accurate but much faster' and 'closer to 100% accurate but slower,' and you can revisit that decision at any time without changing your data or algorithm, just the setting. In FAISS the IVF dial is the index's `nprobe` attribute and the HNSW dial is `index.hnsw.efSearch`; in pgvector they are `ivfflat.probes` and `hnsw.ef_search`.

The tradeoff is also more forgiving than it sounds, because of the clustering property covered earlier: embedding spaces aren't randomly scattered, they're organized into coherent semantic neighborhoods. An ANN algorithm's occasional miss, such as returning the 4th-nearest neighbor instead of the true 3rd, is usually still a relevant result from the same semantic neighborhood, not a random one. For most products (semantic search, recommendation, RAG retrieval), a small recall loss against the exact top-k is imperceptible to an end user, while the latency improvement it buys, which can be orders of magnitude at large scale, is the difference between a system that's usable at production scale and one that isn't.

examples.title: Counting Comparisons: Brute Force vs. IVF
examples.code:
def brute_force_ops(n):
    return n

def ivf_ops(n, nlist, nprobe):
    vectors_per_cluster = n / nlist
    return nlist + nprobe * vectors_per_cluster

n = 1_000_000
nlist = 1000
nprobe = 8

print(brute_force_ops(n))
print(int(ivf_ops(n, nlist, nprobe)))
examples.explanation: brute_force_ops returns n, because exact kNN computes a distance to every one of the n stored vectors. ivf_ops models IVF's two-phase cost: nlist comparisons against the centroids (cheap, since there are far fewer centroids than vectors), plus nprobe clusters' worth of vectors, each cluster holding roughly n / nlist vectors on average. With a million stored vectors, 1000 clusters, and nprobe of 8, the operation count drops from 1,000,000 to 9,000, over a hundredfold reduction, without touching the data or the accuracy of the distance calculation. That's the value of IVF in one comparison: the same distance formula computed far fewer times, because most of the collection is ruled out cheaply via the centroids.

examples.title: A Miniature IVF Search, Step by Step
examples.explanation: ranked_clusters sorts all four centroids by distance to the query, and probed_clusters keeps only the closest nprobe of them: with nprobe=1, that's cluster_a, whose centroid [0.0, 0.0] sits at the query. The inner loop then only ever scans the 3 vectors that belong to cluster_a, never touching the 9 vectors in the other three clusters, and finds [0.1, 0.1] as the nearest vector, having done exactly 3 distance comparisons instead of 12. That's the IVF mechanism at toy scale: the centroid comparison (4 of them, cheap) ruled out three-quarters of the actual vector comparisons before they ever happened. At production scale (millions of vectors, thousands of clusters) the same mechanism is what turns an infeasible linear scan into a search that only touches a small, relevant slice of the collection.

examples.title: A Toy Two-Layer Graph Walk
examples.explanation: The search always starts at a fixed entry point (A) in the sparsest layer. In layer1_edges, A's only connection is the long-range link to D, and D (position 9) is much closer to the query (10) than A (position 0) is, so the greedy walk jumps straight there, giving top_path = ['A', 'D']. That one long-range hop covered most of the numeric distance in a single step, which is what the sparse top layer is for. The search then drops into layer0_edges, starting from D, and checks D's local, densely-connected neighbors (C and E) -- both are farther from the query than D already is, so the loop immediately breaks without moving, giving bottom_path = ['D']. The final result, D, is the nearest node to the query among all six, found by examining only a handful of nodes and never looking at B. A real HNSW graph runs this same two-phase idea -- sparse long-range layer first, dense local layer last -- across many more layers and far more nodes, which is why it scales so much better than checking every node's distance.

misconceptions.description: Approximate nearest neighbor search is just a faster but less careful version of brute-force search -- like scanning fewer stored vectors and hoping for the best.
misconceptions.clarification: ANN algorithms don't look at fewer vectors at random; they invest structured work upfront (clustering into centroids for IVF, building a multi-layer proximity graph for HNSW) specifically so that the small subset of vectors they do examine at query time is very likely to contain the true nearest neighbors. The speedup doesn't come from being sloppy; it comes from using the data's own clustered structure to rule out large swaths of clearly-irrelevant vectors cheaply, via centroids or graph traversal, before ever computing a full distance to most of the collection.

misconceptions.description: Once you switch from brute-force to an ANN algorithm like HNSW or IVF, you've permanently traded away some amount of accuracy for speed, with no way to get more of it back without rebuilding everything from scratch.
misconceptions.clarification: Recall is a live, adjustable dial, not a one-time trade locked in at build time. IVF's nprobe (how many clusters to probe per query) and HNSW's ef_search (how wide a candidate list to keep during the greedy search) can both typically be changed on a per-query basis, without rebuilding the index at all. Raising either one buys back recall at the cost of some additional query latency, for whichever queries need it. The parameters that DO require a full rebuild to change are the ones that shape the index's underlying structure itself (IVF's nlist, or HNSW's M and ef_construction), the distinction the next concept explores in depth.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and what does the comparison tell you about how much work IVF saves relative to brute force at this scale?
exercises.code:
def brute_force_ops(n):
    return n

def ivf_ops(n, nlist, nprobe):
    vectors_per_cluster = n / nlist
    return nlist + nprobe * vectors_per_cluster

n = 1_000_000
nlist = 1000
nprobe = 8

print(brute_force_ops(n))
print(int(ivf_ops(n, nlist, nprobe)))
hints: brute_force_ops returns n, so there's nothing to compute there.
For ivf_ops, work out vectors_per_cluster first (n divided by nlist), then plug into nlist + nprobe * vectors_per_cluster.
int(...) truncates any decimal remainder -- but with these particular numbers, does vectors_per_cluster even come out as a non-whole number in the first place?
exercises.solutionExplanation: brute_force_ops(1_000_000) is 1_000_000: exact kNN costs one comparison per stored vector. For ivf_ops, vectors_per_cluster = 1_000_000 / 1000 = 1000.0, so the total is nlist + nprobe * vectors_per_cluster = 1000 + 8 * 1000 = 9000, and int(9000.0) is 9000 since there's no fractional part to truncate. The comparison, 1,000,000 versus 9,000, shows IVF's core value: at this scale the approximate search does about 1% of the comparisons brute force would, ruling out 99.1% of the collection through the cheap centroid step before computing distances to most stored vectors.

exercises.prompt: A team implements IVF search expecting a big speedup over brute force, but after deploying it, their monitoring shows query latency barely improved at all -- it's almost as slow as the brute-force version it replaced, even though it still returns correct results. Find the bug (tracked here via a `scanned` counter that should stay small, but doesn't).
hints: nprobe is passed into ivf_search as a parameter -- is it actually used anywhere in the function body?
probed_clusters is meant to hold only the nprobe closest clusters, but look closely at what ranked_clusters gets assigned to it -- is anything actually filtering it down?
Compare the scanned count this buggy version reports against what it should be for nprobe=1 with only 3 vectors in the nearest cluster.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is probed_clusters = ranked_clusters: it copies the *entire* sorted list of clusters and ignores the nprobe parameter instead of taking its first nprobe entries. As a result, ivf_search scans every vector in every cluster on every query whatever nprobe is, functionally identical to brute force plus a wasted sort and centroid comparison, which is why the team saw no speedup. It still returns the *correct* nearest vector (buggy: scanned=9), because with nprobe=1 the nearest cluster contains the nearest vector in this toy example. That's why the bug is dangerous: correctness testing wouldn't catch it, only latency or throughput monitoring would, since the result is right but the point of IVF (touching a small fraction of the collection) is defeated. The fix, probed_clusters = ranked_clusters[:nprobe], slices the list to the nprobe closest clusters, dropping scanned from 9 to 3 here and, at production scale with thousands of clusters, from 'scan everything' to 'scan a small, relevant slice,' the reason to use IVF at all.

assessments.prompt: Why do exact spatial index structures like KD-trees, which work well for 2D or 3D spatial data, generally fail to outperform brute-force search for high-dimensional embedding vectors?
options: KD-trees require the data to already be sorted, which embeddings never are.

Their pruning strategy relies on confidently ruling out whole branches of the tree as 'too far away'; in high dimensions, partition boundaries end up close to almost every query, so pruning collapses and the tree ends up visiting nearly every node anyway.
KD-trees only support Euclidean distance, and most embedding models require cosine similarity.
KD-trees only work for data with fewer than 100 stored vectors total.
assessments.explanation: A KD-tree's speed advantage over brute force comes from pruning: looking at a whole branch and confidently deciding 'nothing in here can possibly be closer than what I've already found' without checking every point inside. That confidence depends on a meaningful gap between 'clearly inside this partition' and 'clearly outside it,' and the gap collapses in high dimensions, a consequence of the curse of dimensionality covered earlier, where partition boundaries end up close to nearly every point. The “KD-trees only support Euclidean distance, and most…” option isn't the reason: the degradation comes from dimensionality, not the choice of metric. The “KD-trees require the data to already…” option is fabricated: KD-trees build their own structure from unsorted data. The “KD-trees only work for data with fewer…” option describes a scale limit that isn't the mechanism; the degradation is about dimensionality, not dataset size.

assessments.prompt: In a correctly functioning IVF index with nprobe greater than zero, a stored vector that is genuinely very close to the query is sometimes not returned by the search at all. What specifically causes this?
options: The vector may have been assigned, during the original clustering step, to a cluster whose centroid isn't among the nprobe closest centroids for this particular query -- purely because of where the hard cluster boundary happened to fall.
IVF automatically filters out vectors produced by an older version of the embedding model, even if no such filtering was configured.
IVF silently discards any vector that hasn't been re-normalized immediately before the query is run.
IVF only indexes a random sample of the full collection, so some vectors are permanently unsearchable.
assessments.explanation: This is the 'approximate' part of IVF: clustering partitions the space with hard boundaries, but real data doesn't respect hard boundaries, so a vector can be geometrically close to the query while having been assigned to a different cluster than the query's own nearest centroid. If that vector's cluster isn't among the nprobe clusters actually probed, the search never looks at it, so it's missing from the results even though brute-force search would have found it. The “IVF only indexes a random sample…” option is false -- IVF indexes every stored vector, it just organizes them into clusters rather than scanning all of them per query. The “IVF silently discards any vector that hasn't…” and “IVF automatically filters out vectors produced…” options describe filtering mechanisms IVF doesn't have; nothing about IVF's mechanism involves re-normalization checks or automatic version filtering at query time.

assessments.prompt: In HNSW's layered graph structure, what role does the sparse top layer play during a search, according to the highway/local-streets analogy in the explanation?
options: It stores the exact same vectors as the bottom layer, just rounded to lower numeric precision, purely to speed up early comparisons.
It stores each vector's metadata filters, so that filtered searches can skip the top layer entirely.

It lets a search jump across large distances in the vector space quickly using long-range connections, before dropping into denser lower layers to refine locally near the actual answer -- the way a highway covers distance quickly before switching to local streets.
It acts purely as a fallback, only consulted if the search in the bottom layer fails to converge on any candidate at all.
assessments.explanation: In the highway analogy, the sparse top layer has long-range connections that let a greedy search cover large distances across the space in very few hops, landing near the right neighborhood quickly, after which the search drops down to progressively denser layers to do fine-grained local refinement -- like taking a highway to cover distance and switching to local streets only once near the destination. The “It stores the exact same vectors…” option misdescribes the layers as differing only in numeric precision, which isn't how HNSW's layers are built: they differ in which subset of vectors and connections they contain, not in precision. The “It acts purely as a fallback, only…” option is backwards -- the top layer is used first, not as a fallback. The “It stores each vector's metadata filters…” option is fabricated: metadata filtering isn't part of HNSW's core layered structure as described here.

assessments.prompt: Which statement accurately distinguishes what an ANN algorithm like IVF or HNSW actually does from simply 'scanning fewer vectors at random and hoping for the best'?
options: ANN algorithms guarantee finding the exact mathematical top-k every time, which is precisely what distinguishes them from random sampling.
ANN algorithms examine every single stored vector just like brute force does, but skip the final sorting step to save time.
ANN algorithms and random subset sampling are functionally identical in practice; 'approximate nearest neighbor' is essentially a more technical-sounding name for the same idea.
ANN algorithms invest real, structured work upfront -- clustering into centroids for IVF, or building a multi-layer proximity graph for HNSW.
assessments.explanation: ANN isn't sloppy or lucky: its speedup comes from structured preprocessing (IVF's clustering and centroids, HNSW's layered graph) that uses the data's own clustered structure to rule out large swaths of clearly irrelevant vectors cheaply, before computing a full distance to most of the collection. The “ANN algorithms and random subset sampling…” option collapses a meaningful, structure-driven mechanism into 'the same thing' as random sampling, which the explanation directly rejects. The “ANN algorithms guarantee finding the exact mathematical…” option is wrong by definition: 'approximate' means giving up the guarantee of finding the exact top-k, not securing it; that guarantee belongs to brute-force search instead. The “ANN algorithms examine every single stored vector…” option is factually wrong: the point of ANN algorithms is to avoid examining every stored vector, not to skip sorting at the end.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to someone who has only ever used exact search, why production vector databases give up on finding the mathematically exact nearest neighbors and instead use approximate algorithms like HNSW or IVF -- and why that tradeoff turns out to be far more acceptable in practice than it might sound.
assessments.modelAnswer: Exact brute-force nearest-neighbor search is correct, but comparing the query against every stored vector scales linearly with the collection, which stops being fast enough well before a production system's data reaches millions or hundreds of millions of vectors. Every vector you add adds latency to every query. Classical exact indexes that work well in low dimensions, like KD-trees, don't rescue this, because their pruning relies on a meaningful gap between near and far regions, and that gap collapses once dimensionality reaches the hundreds, the same curse of dimensionality that makes raw high-dimensional intuition unreliable. Approximate algorithms give up the guarantee of the exact top-k in exchange for a cost that grows far more slowly with collection size: IVF clusters the data up front and searches only the clusters nearest the query, while HNSW builds a layered graph that jumps long distances through sparse top layers before refining locally in dense bottom layers. The tradeoff is acceptable, and not just convenient, because embedding spaces are clustered by training rather than randomly scattered: when an approximate search misses the exact best match, what it returns is usually still a relevant neighbor from the same semantic neighborhood. Both algorithms also expose a tunable dial (nprobe, ef_search) for trading a bit more latency for a bit more accuracy on demand, so most products accept a small, controllable recall loss in exchange for serving similarity search at all at real-world scale, rather than treating 'approximate' as a compromise forced on them.

concepts.title: Indexing Parameters, Recall, and the Speed/Accuracy Tradeoff
concepts.description: HNSW and IVF each expose a few parameters (M, ef_construction, ef_search for HNSW; nlist, nprobe for IVF) that trade query latency, recall, memory, and build time against each other. Choosing sane values for production means measuring recall against a brute-force ground truth on a representative sample of real queries, not guessing from a library's defaults.
learningObjectives: Define recall@k for approximate nearest-neighbor search and explain how it's measured against a brute-force ground truth.
Explain the effect of IVF's nprobe on the recall/latency tradeoff, and connect it to the cluster-boundary problem from the previous concept.
Explain the effect of HNSW's ef_search on the recall/latency tradeoff, and why it's the parameter you can safely tune per query without rebuilding anything.
Distinguish parameters that require a full index rebuild to change (nlist, M, ef_construction) from ones that don't (nprobe, ef_search).

Explain, at a conceptual level, how vector quantization (e.g., product quantization) trades some precision for large memory savings, and why it's often combined with IVF rather than used as an alternative to it.
Describe a reasonable process for choosing index parameters for a real production workload.

sections.heading: Recall@k: Turning 'Approximate' Into a Measurable Number
sections.body:
'Approximate' is a measurable claim, not a vague qualifier, and the standard measure is **recall@k**: run a query through both the brute-force exact search and the approximate index, and check what fraction of the exact search's true top-k also appears in the approximate top-k. Average that over many representative queries and you get one number, recall@10 of 0.95, say, that tells you how close your approximate index comes to the exact answer for your data and query patterns.

This measurement isn't optional busywork. Approximate misses tend to look *plausible* because embedding spaces are clustered (as covered in the previous two concepts): an ANN index that misses the true 3rd-nearest neighbor typically returns something from the same semantic neighborhood, not an obviously wrong result. So you can't catch a poorly tuned index by eyeballing whether results 'look reasonable'; you need an exact-search baseline, computed offline on a representative sample, to know whether your index is underperforming.

sections.heading: IVF's Knobs: nlist and nprobe
sections.body:
IVF exposes two parameters with very different roles. `nlist`, the number of clusters, is fixed at build time: changing it means re-clustering the whole collection, a full rebuild. A larger `nlist` means finer-grained clusters, which narrows each search once you know which clusters to probe, but also means more cluster boundaries for true nearest neighbors to fall on the wrong side of.

`nprobe`, the number of clusters scanned per query, is the parameter you tune live, often per query, with no rebuild. Recall the cluster-boundary problem from the previous concept: a nearby vector can be assigned to a cluster other than the one closest to the query, because of where the hard boundary fell during clustering. Raising `nprobe` buys back that lost recall by also checking the next-most-likely clusters 'just in case,' at the cost of scanning more vectors and so more latency. At the extreme, `nprobe = nlist` (probing every cluster) degenerates into brute force with extra overhead; the point of a smaller `nprobe` is to trade some guaranteed correctness for speed, in a way you can dial in. A commonly cited starting point for `nlist` is a small multiple of the square root of the number of vectors; treat it as a place to begin the sweep, not an answer.

sections.heading: HNSW's Knobs: M, ef_construction, and ef_search
sections.body:
HNSW's three parameters split the same way. `M`, the maximum number of graph connections each node keeps per layer, and `ef_construction`, the candidate list size used only while *building* the graph, both shape the structure of the graph itself -- more connections and a more thorough build process produce a more accurate, more robust graph, at the cost of more memory (M directly multiplies how many edges get stored) and a slower one-time build. Changing either one means rebuilding the entire graph.

`ef_search`, the candidate list size kept during the greedy search at *query* time, is different: a per-query knob you can change without touching the graph. A larger `ef_search` keeps a wider set of 'good enough so far' candidates alive as the search walks the graph, instead of committing early to the first local optimum it finds, which raises the chance of finding the true nearest neighbors at the cost of more comparisons and latency per query. (Keep it at least as large as k; in many implementations a smaller value limits how many results you can get back.) Because it can change instantly, per request, with no rebuild, it's the dial you reach for in production: an interactive user waiting on a response might tolerate a lower `ef_search` for lower latency, while an offline batch job might afford a higher one for better recall, on the same graph.

sections.heading: Memory, Build Time, and Quantization
sections.body:
Query latency and recall aren't the only resources in tension: memory footprint and build and maintenance time matter too, and they don't always move with the query-time tradeoffs. HNSW graphs store multiple edges per vector across layers, so memory scales with both `M` and the collection size; a large, high-`M` graph can use significantly more memory than the raw vectors it indexes. IVF is more memory-frugal per vector, but its centroids need periodic re-training as the data distribution drifts: if your embeddings' overall shape shifts (new content categories, a model upgrade), months-old centroids may no longer reflect where the data clusters, degrading recall until someone notices and rebuilds them.

When a collection grows large enough that even the footprint of full-precision vectors (typically 4 bytes per dimension, as 32-bit floats) doesn't comfortably fit in memory, **quantization** becomes relevant: instead of storing each vector at full precision, compress it into a small number of quantized codes, looked up from a set of learned reference vectors ('codebooks') -- **product quantization (PQ)** is the most common approach, splitting each vector into sub-vectors and quantizing each sub-vector independently. This trades a bit of precision in distance calculations (and therefore, again, some recall) for a large reduction in memory footprint (an order of magnitude or more; the example below reaches 48x), which can be the difference between a collection fitting in RAM or not. In practice, quantization is usually paired *with* IVF rather than treated as a competing alternative -- an 'IVF-PQ' index uses IVF's clustering to narrow the candidate set, then PQ's compact, quantized representation to store and compare vectors within that narrowed set cheaply, stacking two independent tradeoffs (which clusters to check, and how precisely to represent each vector) rather than picking just one.

sections.heading: Choosing Parameters for a Real Workload
sections.body:
No parameter has a universally correct default: the right values depend on your data's clustering structure and your query patterns, both of which vary by application. The reliable process: take a representative sample of real (or realistically distributed) queries and compute their true top-k results via brute force once, offline, as ground truth. Then sweep a range of candidate settings (several `nprobe` or `ef_search` values), run the same queries through the approximate index at each, and plot recall@k against measured query latency (look at a high percentile like p99, not just the average, since tail latency is usually what violates a product's requirements). Pick the setting that clears your latency budget with acceptable recall, not the one that maximizes recall unconditionally, since recall past what your product needs (especially with a reranking step downstream that would catch minor ordering differences) is latency and cost spent for no user benefit.

One last easy-to-forget point: this evaluation is tied to your specific data and model. If you swap embedding models, or your data's distribution shifts meaningfully over time (new categories of content, a big influx of a particular document type), the recall behavior of a given parameter setting can shift too : recall is a property of how well your parameters match your *current data*, not a fixed property of `nprobe=8` or `ef_search=100` in the abstract. Re-run the measurement after any such change, rather than assuming old tuning still holds.

examples.title: Measuring Recall@3 as nprobe Changes
examples.explanation: true_top3 is computed once, via brute force over all 12 points, and never changes: it's the ground truth this example measures against. At nprobe=1, only the single closest cluster (B) gets probed, and IVF's top-3 comes out as ['b2', 'b4', 'b1'] -- correct on 2 of the 3 true nearest points, missing a2 (which belongs to cluster A) entirely, since cluster A was never probed. That gives recall@3 of 0.667. At nprobe=2, cluster A also gets probed, a2 becomes visible, and it correctly displaces b1 from the top 3 -- recall@3 reaches a perfect 1.0. Bumping nprobe to 3 (probing every cluster) changes nothing further, since recall was already perfect and cluster C's points were never competitive. This is the cluster-boundary problem from the previous concept, made concrete and measurable: a2 was always close enough to matter, but IVF's hard cluster boundaries hid it until nprobe was raised enough to look in the right place.

examples.title: Why Memory Footprint Forces the Quantization Question
examples.code:
def gb(num_bytes):
    return round(num_bytes / (1024 ** 3), 1)

n = 50_000_000       # 50 million stored vectors, a large production collection
dim = 768

full_precision_bytes_per_vector = dim * 4   # float32: 4 bytes per dimension
pq_bytes_per_vector = 64                    # e.g. 64 sub-quantizers, 1 byte code each

full_total = n * full_precision_bytes_per_vector
pq_total = n * pq_bytes_per_vector

print(gb(full_total), "GB full precision")
print(gb(pq_total), "GB with product quantization")
print(round(full_total / pq_total, 1), "x smaller")
examples.explanation: At 768 dimensions and 4 bytes per dimension (the standard float32 representation), 50 million vectors alone take up about 143 GB, before even accounting for an HNSW graph's extra edge storage or an IVF index's centroids sitting on top of that. Compressing each vector down to 64 quantized bytes via product quantization (splitting the 768-dimensional vector into 64 sub-vectors and representing each as a one-byte code looked up from a learned codebook) drops the same collection to about 3 GB, a roughly 48x reduction. That's often the difference between a collection fitting in one machine's RAM (fast) and having to be sharded across machines or partly paged from disk (slower and more complex), independent of query speed. The cost is what you'd expect: comparing lossy quantized representations is a less precise stand-in for comparing the original vectors, which shows up as somewhat lower recall unless compensated for. It's one more axis in the same speed/accuracy/memory tradeoff.

misconceptions.description: You should always set nprobe (or ef_search) as high as your system can tolerate, so the index is 'as accurate as possible' -- there's no real downside to erring toward more accuracy.
misconceptions.clarification: Recall past what your product needs isn't free: every increase in nprobe or ef_search adds real query latency and compute cost, for a diminishing (and eventually negligible) improvement in result quality, especially once a downstream reranking step would catch minor ordering differences anyway. Treating maximum recall as the automatic goal, rather than 'good enough recall within our latency budget,' means paying ongoing latency and infrastructure cost for accuracy improvements users will never perceive. The right target is measured against your actual product's tolerance, not maximized unconditionally.

misconceptions.description: Once you've tuned nprobe or ef_search using a recall measurement, that setting is correct permanently, since it's a property of the algorithm's parameters.
misconceptions.clarification: Recall is a property of how well a given parameter setting matches your CURRENT data's clustering structure and your CURRENT query patterns, not a fixed, timeless property of a number like nprobe=8. If the embedding model changes, or the underlying data distribution shifts meaningfully (new content categories, a big influx of a different document type), the same parameter value can produce meaningfully different recall than it did when you first measured it, because the data it's now operating over has different structure. Re-measuring recall after any such change, rather than assuming an old tuning result still holds indefinitely, is part of operating one of these indexes correctly, not an optional extra step.
misconceptions.fact: Recall is a property of how well a given parameter setting matches your CURRENT data's clustering structure and your CURRENT query patterns, not a fixed, timeless property of a number like nprobe=8.

exercises.prompt: Using the IVF simulation and recall_at_3 function from the explanation above, what does the loop print for nprobe = 1, 2, and 3, and why does recall change (or not) between them?
hints: First work out which cluster centroid (A, B, or C) is closest to the query (3.0, 0.1) -- that's the only cluster probed when nprobe=1.
true_top3 is computed once, via brute force over ALL points, regardless of nprobe -- it doesn't change across the loop iterations. Only which clusters get probed changes.
Check whether a2 (which is assigned to cluster A) is actually one of the 3 closest points overall to the query -- and whether cluster A is among the clusters probed at each nprobe value.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Cluster B's centroid (5.0, 0.0) is closest to the query (3.0, 0.1), so at nprobe=1, only cluster B's points (b1 through b4) are ever considered. b2 and b4 correctly come out on top (they really are the two closest points overall), but the true 3rd-closest point is a2, which belongs to cluster A and is never considered at nprobe=1, so IVF's top-3 falls back to the next-best point it CAN see, b1, giving recall@3 of 2/3, about 0.667. At nprobe=2, cluster A (the next-closest centroid to the query) also gets probed, which makes a2 visible to the search, and it displaces b1 from the top 3, and recall@3 reaches a perfect 1.0. Raising nprobe to 3 (probing every cluster, including the distant cluster C) doesn't change anything further, because none of cluster C's points are competitive. Recall was already perfect at nprobe=2, so nprobe=3 only adds comparisons against cluster C for no benefit. This is the cluster-boundary problem made concrete: a2 was always geometrically close enough to matter, but IVF's hard cluster boundaries initially hid it from the search entirely, and only a higher nprobe recovered it.

exercises.solutionCode:
true_top3 = ["b2", "b4", "a2"]
approx_nprobe1 = ["b2", "b4", "b1"]
approx_nprobe2 = ["b2", "b4", "a2"]

def recall_at_k(true_ids, approx_ids):
    true_set = set(true_ids)
    approx_set = set(approx_ids)
    return len(true_set & approx_set) / len(true_set)

print(recall_at_k(true_top3, approx_nprobe1))
print(recall_at_k(true_top3, approx_nprobe2))
exercises.solutionExplanation: recall_at_k converts both lists to sets and intersects them: set(true_ids) & set(approx_ids) contains exactly the ids that show up in both the true top-k and the approximate top-k. Dividing the size of that intersection by len(true_ids), the number of true results (which is what 'k' refers to), gives the fraction of the true top-k that the approximate search actually managed to find. For approx_nprobe1 = ['b2', 'b4', 'b1'], only 'b2' and 'b4' overlap with true_top3, so recall_at_k returns 2/3, about 0.667; for approx_nprobe2 = ['b2', 'b4', 'a2'], all three ids overlap, so it returns 1.0. This is the metric a production evaluation would compute, applied here by hand to a tiny example instead of averaged automatically across thousands of held-out queries against a real brute-force baseline.

exercises.prompt: This function measures recall@k of an approximate index against exact search: the share of the true top-k neighbours that the ANN result also found. The ANN result below finds 2 of the 3 true neighbours, so recall should be 0.67, but it prints 1.0. Find and fix the bug.

    exact_top = exact_ids[:k]
    ann_top = ann_ids[:k]
    found = [i for i in ann_top if i in ann_top]
    return round(len(found) / k, 2)

exact = ["d1", "d2", "d3", "d4"]

Recall asks: of the true neighbours, how many did the approximate search return?
Compare the ANN ids with the exact ids, not with themselves.
exercises.solutionCode:
def recall_at_k(exact_ids, ann_ids, k):
    exact_top = set(exact_ids[:k])
    ann_top = ann_ids[:k]
    found = [i for i in ann_top if i in exact_top]
    return round(len(found) / k, 2)

exact = ["d1", "d2", "d3", "d4"]
ann = ["d1", "d3", "d9", "d2"]
print(recall_at_k(exact, ann, 3))   # 0.67
exercises.solutionExplanation: The comprehension tested each ANN id for membership in `ann_top` itself, which is always true, so recall was always 1.0 and the index looked perfect. Recall@k must compare the approximate top-k with the exact top-k: here d1 and d3 are in both, d9 is not a true neighbour, and d2 fell just outside the ANN top 3, so recall is 2/3. Using a set for the exact ids also makes lookups fast. A metric that cannot fail is worse than no metric, because it hides real recall loss when you tune parameters like ef or nprobe.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following index parameters can typically be changed for an individual query, without rebuilding the underlying index structure at all?
options: HNSW's M and IVF's nlist
HNSW's ef_search and IVF's nprobe
None of them -- every index parameter requires a full rebuild to change
HNSW's ef_construction and IVF's nlist
assessments.explanation: ef_search (HNSW) and nprobe (IVF) both control how much work is done at query time, within an already-built index structure -- widening the candidate list during graph traversal, or probing more clusters -- and neither one changes the structure itself, so both can be adjusted freely, even per individual query. M and ef_construction (“HNSW's M and IVF's nlist” and “HNSW's ef_construction and IVF's nlist”) shape the HNSW graph's actual connections and are baked in when the graph is built; nlist (“HNSW's M and IVF's nlist” and “HNSW's ef_construction and IVF's nlist”) determines how the data was originally clustered for IVF. Changing any of those three requires rebuilding the corresponding index from scratch, which is why the correct answer is the set of parameters you can tune live in a running production system.

assessments.prompt: A team reports that their ANN index has a measured recall@10 of 0.95 against a brute-force ground truth. What does that number actually mean?
options: On average across the queries measured, 95% of the true top-10 nearest neighbors (as found by brute-force search) also appeared in the ANN index's own top-10 results.
The ANN index runs about 95% faster than an equivalent brute-force search over the same collection.
95% of all vectors in the entire collection were included when the index was originally built.
The index returns exactly 10 results for 95% of the queries it handles.
assessments.explanation: Recall@k is defined as the correct answer says: run a query through both brute-force (the ground truth) and the approximate index, check what fraction of the true top-k also shows up in the approximate top-k, and average that fraction across many representative queries. The “The index returns exactly 10 results…” option confuses recall with a claim about result-count consistency, which isn't what recall measures. The “The ANN index runs about 95% faster…” option conflates recall (an accuracy measurement) with latency (a speed measurement): these are two separate axes you plot against each other, not the same number. The “95% of all vectors in the entire…” option describes something about index construction coverage, not about how well the index's query results match ground truth.

assessments.prompt: Product quantization (PQ) is typically deployed as part of an 'IVF-PQ' index rather than as a standalone replacement for IVF. Why?
options: 'IVF-PQ' is purely a marketing label; using PQ alone would produce identical memory savings and identical recall to using it alongside IVF.
PQ replaces the need for any distance metric entirely, so it must be paired with an algorithm like IVF that still computes one.
IVF and PQ address two independent tradeoffs -- which clusters to search, and how precisely to represent each vector.
PQ can only compress vectors that have already been assigned to an IVF cluster; it has no defined behavior when applied to vectors that haven't been clustered first.
assessments.explanation: IVF and PQ are two independent tradeoffs: IVF's clustering narrows down which vectors get compared at all, while PQ's compressed representation reduces the memory and computation cost of each individual comparison. Combining them as IVF-PQ stacks both benefits rather than duplicating one. The “PQ can only compress vectors that have…” option invents a technical dependency that doesn't exist: PQ's compression scheme (splitting a vector into sub-vectors and quantizing each independently) works on any vector, clustered or not. The “PQ replaces the need for any distance…” option misdescribes PQ's role: it changes how vectors are represented and compared, not whether a distance metric is needed. The “'IVF-PQ' is purely a marketing label; using…” option is wrong because using PQ alone (without IVF's narrowing step) would still require scanning the same number of vectors, just each one more cheaply. The memory savings from PQ are real either way, but IVF's speed benefit from narrowing the candidate set would be lost.

assessments.prompt: A team measures good recall for a given ef_search value against a brute-force baseline and considers the tuning finished permanently. Under what circumstance would that assumption break down?
options: The assumption only breaks down if the total number of stored vectors decreases, since recall tuning is exclusively sensitive to shrinking collections.
It never breaks down -- recall is a fixed mathematical property of the parameter value itself, independent of the underlying data.
The assumption only breaks down if the underlying server hardware is upgraded to a faster machine.

If the embedding model changes, or the underlying data distribution shifts meaningfully over time, the same ef_search value can produce meaningfully different recall than what was originally measured, because recall reflects how well the parameter matches the CURRENT data's clustering structure.
assessments.explanation: Recall is a property of how well a parameter setting matches the data's current clustering structure and query patterns, not a fixed, timeless property of the number itself. If the embedding model changes or the data distribution shifts (new content categories, an influx of a different document type), the same ef_search value can behave quite differently than it did when first measured, because the underlying structure it's operating over has changed. The “It never breaks down -- recall…” option directly contradicts this. The “The assumption only breaks down if the total…” option invents a one-directional dependency (shrinking only): growth or compositional shifts matter just as much as shrinkage. The “The assumption only breaks down if the underlying…” option confuses hardware speed, which affects latency, with recall, which is about accuracy relative to ground truth and is not a hardware-dependent property.

assessments.prompt: A teammate proposes always setting nprobe (or ef_search) to the maximum the system can handle, arguing 'more accuracy is always better, so why not just max it out?' Explain why this isn't automatically the right default, and describe how you'd actually go about choosing a value for a production system.
assessments.modelAnswer: Maximizing nprobe or ef_search does push recall higher, but at a real cost in query latency and compute that accrues on every query, for diminishing returns: past a certain point, extra recall doesn't change what users experience, especially if a reranking step downstream smooths over minor ordering differences. Treating 'maximum accuracy' as the default ignores that recall only matters insofar as it serves a product requirement; beyond that, you pay latency and infrastructure cost for no perceptible benefit, which is a real cost at production query volumes. The way to choose is to measure, not guess: take a representative sample of real queries, compute their true top-k via brute force once as ground truth, sweep a range of candidate nprobe or ef_search values, and measure both recall@k and query latency (especially a high percentile like p99, since tail latency usually causes the user-facing problems) at each. Pick the smallest value that clears your latency budget while meeting the recall target your use case needs, and revisit the measurement whenever the embedding model changes or the data distribution shifts, since the right setting is tied to your current data, not a universal constant.

concepts.title: Metadata Filtering and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
concepts.description: Production vector search is almost never pure similarity search: it has to respect structured constraints like tenant, permissions, or recency at the same time, and how you combine those constraints with an ANN index has correctness and performance consequences. Filtered retrieval plus an LLM is also the mechanical foundation of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
learningObjectives: Explain why pure vector similarity search is usually insufficient in production, and identify the security-relevant risk of ignoring metadata constraints like tenant or permissions.
Distinguish post-filtering from pre-filtering, and explain the failure mode where post-filtering returns fewer than k results, with no error, even when matching data exists.
Explain the performance tradeoff naive pre-filtering makes, and why filter selectivity determines whether it's a good approach.
Describe, at a conceptual level, how production vector databases integrate filtering into ANN traversal itself, rather than treating it as a separate step.
Describe the end-to-end RAG pipeline (chunking, embedding, filtered retrieval, prompt assembly, generation) and explain what problem it solves for an LLM.
Connect a concrete retrieval failure (poor recall, mismatched embedding models, a missed filter) to a downstream RAG hallucination, and explain why that's a retrieval bug, not a generation bug.

sections.heading: Why Similarity Alone Isn't Enough
sections.body:
Everything so far answers 'which stored vectors are semantically closest to this query,' but almost no production system can stop there. A multi-tenant SaaS product needs results scoped to the current customer's documents. An internal knowledge base has to respect who may see what, document by document. A news or support search often needs to prefer, or strictly require, recent content. None of that is a similarity question; it's an ordinary structured constraint of the kind you'd write a WHERE clause for in SQL.

Pure top-k nearest-neighbor search knows nothing about any of this. Unfiltered, it returns the most semantically similar vector in the *entire* index, whatever tenant it belongs to or whoever is allowed to see it. That's more than a relevance annoyance: it's a documented class of security bug in production RAG and search systems. An index that isn't scoped correctly by permissions can leak another tenant's or user's private content into search results or, worse, into an LLM's context window, simply because that content was the closest match to someone else's query. Metadata filtering isn't a nice-to-have on top of vector search; for most real systems it's a hard correctness requirement, enforced on every query.

sections.heading: Post-Filtering: Simple, and Silently Broken at the Edges
sections.body:
The most obvious way to combine similarity search with a metadata constraint is **post-filtering**: run the ANN top-k search as usual, ignoring the filter, then filter the k candidates by whatever metadata condition you need (tenant, permissions, date). It's simple to implement and wrong in an easy-to-miss way: if few or none of the true top-k closest vectors satisfy the filter, you get back fewer than k results, or zero, *even though plenty of matching, relevant documents exist elsewhere in the collection*, further down the unfiltered ranking than the ANN search looked.

```python
import math

def dist(a, b):
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)))

query = (0.0, 0.0)

# (vector, tenant) pairs: five documents belong to a large, active tenant;
# only one belongs to the tenant actually making this request
documents = {
    "doc1": ((0.1, 0.1), "tenant_big"),
    "doc2": ((0.2, 0.0), "tenant_big"),
    "doc3": ((0.3, 0.1), "tenant_big"),
    "doc4": ((0.4, 0.0), "tenant_big"),
    "doc5": ((0.5, 0.1), "tenant_big"),
    "doc6": ((0.6, 0.0), "tenant_small"),
}

def ann_top_k(query, k):
    return sorted(documents, key=lambda name: dist(query, documents[name][0]))[:k]

def post_filter_search(query, tenant, k):
    candidates = ann_top_k(query, k)               # filter ignored during the ANN step
    return [name for name in candidates if documents[name][1] == tenant]

print(post_filter_search(query, "tenant_small", k=5))   # []
```

tenant_small's only document, doc6, is the 6th-closest match overall, but `ann_top_k(query, k=5)` looks only at the 5 closest documents *overall*, all of which belong to tenant_big, so doc6 never enters the candidate pool that gets filtered. The result is an empty list, with no error, for a tenant that has relevant content in the index. This bug is easy to miss in testing because it appears only when the requesting tenant's documents are a small minority of the collection; a test environment where one test tenant dominates the index will never surface it.

sections.heading: Pre-Filtering: Correct, but Its Speed Depends on Selectivity
sections.body:
The fix for this failure is **pre-filtering**: restrict the candidates to vectors satisfying the metadata condition *first*, then search for nearest neighbors within that subset.

```python
def pre_filter_search(query, tenant, k):
    candidates = [name for name in documents if documents[name][1] == tenant]
    return sorted(candidates, key=lambda name: dist(query, documents[name][0]))[:k]

print(pre_filter_search(query, "tenant_small", k=5))   # ['doc6']
```

This finds doc6, because the filter-agnostic ranking never gets the chance to hide it. But look at what pre_filter_search does: it filters to the matching subset, then computes a distance to *every member of that subset*, a brute-force scan over the filtered candidates, not an ANN search. That's fine, and arguably free, when the filter is highly selective (a small subset of the collection): scanning a small subset is cheap regardless. But most ANN structures, HNSW's graph and IVF's clusters, are built once over the *entire* collection, not per filter value. If the filter barely narrows the collection (say, a boolean flag true for 90% of documents), naive pre-filtering degenerates toward scanning almost the whole collection, losing the ANN speedup you built the index for. But look at what pre_filter_search is actually doing under the hood: it filters down to the matching subset, then computes a distance to *every single member of that subset directly* -- a brute-force scan over the filtered candidates, not an ANN search at all. That's completely fine, and arguably free, when the filter is highly selective (a small subset of the total collection): scanning a small filtered subset directly is cheap regardless. But most ANN index structures -- HNSW's graph, IVF's clusters -- are built once, over the *entire* collection, not separately per possible filter value; if the filter barely narrows the collection down at all (say, a boolean flag that's true for 90% of documents), naive pre-filtering degenerates back toward scanning almost the whole collection directly, having lost the ANN speedup you built the index for in the first place.

sections.heading: What Production Vector Databases Actually Do
sections.body:
Mature vector databases generally don't force a choice between these two naive strategies; they build filtering into the ANN traversal. One common approach is **filtered graph traversal**: during HNSW's greedy walk, check each candidate node's metadata against the filter, skip non-matching nodes without ending the search, and keep walking past them to explore the graph, instead of ignoring the filter (post-filtering) or restricting the graph to matching nodes ahead of time (which would need a separate graph per filter value). Another approach, better suited to filters with a small number of known, low-cardinality values, is **separate partitioned indexes per common filter value**, such as one HNSW graph per tenant if the tenant count is manageable and known ahead of time. That trades index-management complexity for indexes that need no runtime filtering, since every vector in a tenant's graph already belongs to that tenant.

The engineering principle: the right filtering strategy is an architectural decision that depends on filter **selectivity** (how much of the collection the filter rules out) and **cardinality** (how many distinct filter values exist), not a detail to leave to a library's default without checking.

sections.heading: RAG: Where Retrieval Meets Generation
sections.body:
**Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** is the very common application that ties this subject together into one pipeline. Offline, ahead of time: split your source documents into **chunks**, a design decision in its own right, since chunks that are too large dilute relevance and waste the LLM's limited context window on irrelevant surrounding text, while chunks that are too small lose the context a reader (or the LLM) needs to make sense of them. Embed each chunk with a consistent embedding model and store the vector in a vector database alongside metadata: source document, permissions, timestamp, whatever your filtering needs.

Then, online, for each user query: embed the query with that *same* embedding model (the 'don't mix embedding model versions' rule from the first concept, now a hard requirement); run a filtered ANN search, scoped to the requesting user's permissions or tenant, to retrieve the top-k most relevant chunks; and assemble a prompt that includes the retrieved chunk text alongside the user's question. The prompt goes to an LLM, which generates an answer grounded in the retrieved content, often with citations back to the source chunks.

```python
def build_prompt(question, retrieved_chunks):
    context = "\n\n".join(
        f"[Source: {chunk['source']}]\n{chunk['text']}"
        for chunk in retrieved_chunks
    )
    return (
        "Answer the question using ONLY the context below. "
        "If the context does not contain the answer, say you do not know.\n\n"
        f"Context:\n{context}\n\n"
        f"Question: {question}"
    )
```

The pipeline is worth building, instead of asking an LLM the question directly, because a general-purpose LLM's knowledge is fixed at training time, it has no access to your private or current data, and it can't cite a source for a claim it wasn't given. RAG sidesteps that without retraining: it puts the current, relevant facts in the model's context window at request time, for the specific question asked, so the same general-purpose model can answer questions about your own private, frequently changing corpus.

sections.heading: When Retrieval Fails, Generation Looks Like It's Hallucinating
sections.body:
A failure mode trips up many teams building their first RAG system: when the output is wrong (a confidently wrong answer, a citation that doesn't support the claim), the instinct is to blame the LLM, since it produced the final text. But a large share of real RAG failures are **retrieval** bugs in a generation costume: mismatched embedding model versions between index build and query time (meaningless similarity scores), an ANN index tuned for too little recall to retrieve the one chunk that contains the answer, or a filtering bug that leaks in irrelevant or wrong-tenant context.

This produces *confident*, plausible-sounding wrong answers, not an obvious error, because the LLM can't know its retrieved context is bad. It isn't told 'these chunks might be irrelevant, hedge accordingly'; it's handed whatever retrieval produced and asked to answer from it, and a capable model will confidently synthesize an answer from irrelevant context, which makes the failure look like 'the LLM hallucinated' instead of 'retrieval failed upstream.' Debugging a RAG system that gives bad answers should start by inspecting what got retrieved for the failing query, not by assuming generation is at fault.

examples.title: Post-Filtering: An Empty Result Despite Matching Data Existing
examples.explanation: ann_top_k(query, k=5), run without any awareness of tenant, returns doc1 through doc5, the five documents closest to the query overall, all of which happen to belong to tenant_big. post_filter_search then filters that already-fixed list of 5 down to tenant_small's documents, and finds none, because doc6 (tenant_small's only document, and the 6th-closest overall) was never in the candidate list to begin with. The function returns an empty list, with no error or warning, for a tenant that has perfectly good, relevant content sitting in the collection. Increasing k in the initial ANN call would eventually surface doc6, but that requires knowing in advance how far down the unfiltered ranking you might need to look, which depends on exactly how rare the requesting tenant's documents are relative to the rest of the index, information you don't generally have ahead of time, and which can change as the collection grows.

examples.title: Pre-Filtering Finds It, at the Cost of Scanning the Filtered Subset
examples.explanation: pre_filter_search restricts the candidate set to tenant_small's documents -- just doc6 here -- before ranking anything, so doc6 is guaranteed to be considered no matter how far down the unfiltered, whole-collection ranking it would have fallen. Run side by side against the same query and tenant, post_filter_search returns [] while pre_filter_search correctly returns ['doc6']. The tradeoff shows at real scale: pre_filter_search computes dist() against every document belonging to the tenant, with no ANN index accelerating that step. That's fine when a tenant's documents are a small slice of a huge multi-tenant collection, but if a filter matched 80% of a huge collection, the same approach would scan most of the index by hand, defeating the purpose of building an ANN index.

examples.title: Assembling a Grounded Prompt from Retrieved Chunks
examples.code:
def build_prompt(question, retrieved_chunks):
    context = "\n\n".join(
        f"[Source: {chunk['source']}]\n{chunk['text']}"
        for chunk in retrieved_chunks
    )
    return (
        "Answer the question using ONLY the context below. "
        "If the context does not contain the answer, say you do not know.\n\n"
        f"Context:\n{context}\n\n"
        f"Question: {question}"
    )

retrieved_chunks = [
    {"source": "handbook.md#section-4", "text": "Employees accrue 1.5 vacation days per month."},
    {"source": "handbook.md#section-7", "text": "Unused vacation days roll over up to a cap of 10 days."},
]

prompt = build_prompt("How many vacation days do I get per year?", retrieved_chunks)
print(prompt)
examples.explanation: build_prompt takes the chunks the filtered ANN search retrieved (two handbook excerpts here, standing in for a real filtered top-k result) and stitches them into one context block, each labeled with its source, followed by an instruction to answer only from that context, followed by the user's question. This is the mechanical core of RAG: everything about embeddings, distance metrics, ANN indexes, and filtering earlier in this subject exists to produce this retrieved_chunks list correctly and efficiently, and the LLM call itself (not shown, since it just takes this finished prompt string) is almost an afterthought by comparison. Note the 'using ONLY the context below... if the context does not contain the answer, say you do not know' instruction: it's a common prompting pattern that tries to keep the model grounded in what was retrieved instead of its general training-time knowledge, which is the behavior RAG is trying to add. It reduces, but doesn't eliminate, answers that go beyond the context.

misconceptions.description: As long as the embedding similarity search returns the right general topic, it doesn't matter much whether metadata filtering (tenant, permissions) happens before or after the similarity ranking -- it's just an implementation detail.
misconceptions.clarification: The order changes correctness, not just performance. Filtering after an unfiltered top-k ANN search (post-filtering) can silently return fewer than k results -- or zero -- whenever the true top-k semantically-closest vectors happen not to satisfy the filter, even though plenty of matching, relevant documents exist elsewhere in the collection; the ANN step simply never looked far enough to find them. Filtering before searching (pre-filtering) avoids that specific failure by construction, but naive implementations pay for that correctness with speed, since it typically means scanning the filtered subset directly rather than benefiting from the ANN index's usual speedup. This is why production vector databases build filtering into the ANN traversal itself, rather than treating pre- versus post-filtering as two equally fine implementation choices.

misconceptions.description: If a RAG system gives a confidently wrong answer, the LLM's generation step must be the thing that's broken -- it 'hallucinated,' so the fix belongs in prompt engineering or model choice.
misconceptions.clarification: A large share of real-world RAG failures are retrieval bugs that only become visible once generation happens on top of them: a mismatched embedding model version between index-build time and query time, an ANN index tuned for too little recall for how precisely the use case needs to retrieve, or a filtering bug that leaks in irrelevant context. The LLM has no way to know its retrieved context is bad; it's simply handed whatever text retrieval produced and asked to answer using it, and a capable model will confidently synthesize a plausible-sounding answer from irrelevant context just as readily as from good context. Diagnosing a bad RAG answer should start by inspecting exactly what got retrieved for that specific query, before assuming the fault lies in generation.
