exercises.solutionExplanation: The code took the overall top 2 (two shipping chunks) and only then removed non-billing ones, leaving nothing at all; with a slightly different query it would return just one. This is the post-filtering trap: when the filter is selective, the top-k is mostly thrown away. Filtering first (pre-filtering, which vector databases support through metadata filters in the query) guarantees k results from the allowed set when they exist. If a system can only post-filter, it must over-fetch, for example retrieve 10k and then filter, but pre-filtering is the correct default.

assessments.prompt: A search feature runs an unfiltered ANN search for the top 5 nearest documents, then filters that list of 5 down to only documents the requesting user has permission to see. For a user who can only see a small fraction of the overall collection, what is the most likely observable problem with this design?
options: It will frequently return fewer than 5 results -- sometimes zero.
It will raise an exception when no permitted documents appear in the initial top 5.
It will return documents the user isn't permitted to see, since the filter is applied too late to matter.
It will run noticeably slower than an equivalent brute-force search.
assessments.explanation: This is post-filtering, and its well-known failure mode is this: filtering happens after the ANN step already committed to a fixed top-5, unfiltered candidate list, so if few or none of the user's permitted documents happen to be among the overall 5 closest matches, the final filtered result comes back with fewer than 5 items, or none at all, even though the user's permitted documents include perfectly relevant matches sitting further down the unfiltered ranking. The “It will run noticeably slower…” option is wrong: post-filtering is normally cheaper, not slower, than pre-filtering, because it still benefits from the ANN index's speedup on the initial (unfiltered) search. The “It will return documents the user isn't…” option describes the opposite problem: post-filtering, applied correctly, does remove documents the user can't see, it just does so too late to recover documents it should have found instead; it doesn't leak anything unpermitted here. The “It will raise an exception…” option is wrong because the code in question (a simple list-comprehension filter) doesn't raise on an empty result; it returns an empty or short list, which is what makes this bug easy to miss.

assessments.prompt: A vector database applies pre-filtering for a boolean metadata flag that happens to be true for 90% of the entire collection. What's the likely performance consequence?
options: Pre-filtering becomes faster than usual in this case, since fewer vectors technically need to be considered.
Pre-filtering will return incorrect results whenever a filter matches more than 50% of the collection.
Pre-filtering has no performance cost regardless of filter selectivity, since by construction it is always at least as fast as post-filtering.
Pre-filtering degenerates toward directly scanning almost the entire collection.
assessments.explanation: Naive pre-filtering's speed depends on filter selectivity: it restricts to the matching subset first, then scans that subset directly (brute-force, not via the ANN index), which is cheap only when the filter rules out most of the collection. A filter that barely narrows anything down, like a boolean flag true for 90% of documents, means pre-filtering ends up scanning almost the whole collection, defeating the purpose of building an ANN index. The “Pre-filtering becomes faster than usual…” option gets the direction backwards for a filter that matches almost everything, like this one. The “Pre-filtering will return incorrect results whenever…” option invents a correctness threshold that doesn't exist: pre-filtering remains correct regardless of selectivity, it just gets slower. The “Pre-filtering has no performance cost regardless…” option is false: the explanation frames pre-filtering's cost as selectivity-dependent, not uniformly cheap.

assessments.prompt: Mature production vector databases often build metadata filtering directly into ANN traversal rather than choosing purely between naive pre-filtering and post-filtering. Which of the following describes one real approach to this, as covered in the explanation?
options: Run the same unfiltered ANN search twice, independently, and intersect the two resulting sets of candidates.
During HNSW's greedy graph walk, skip nodes that don't match the filter without terminating the search early, and continue exploring the graph past them.
Convert the metadata filter into a query against a separate relational database and discard the vector index's results entirely.
Append the metadata value as an extra numeric dimension directly onto each embedding vector, turning the filter into an ordinary part of the distance calculation.
assessments.explanation: The explanation calls this 'filtered graph traversal': check each candidate node's metadata against the filter as part of HNSW's normal greedy walk, skip non-matching nodes without stopping the search, and keep walking past them to continue exploring the graph, integrating the filter into traversal instead of treating it as a separate before/after step. The “Append the metadata value as an extra…” option describes a technique not mentioned anywhere in the explanation and would corrupt the geometry the distance calculation depends on. The “Run the same unfiltered ANN search twice…” option would not reliably solve the problem post-filtering already has, since running the identical unfiltered search twice would just return the identical unfiltered top-k twice. The “Convert the metadata filter into a query…” option describes discarding the vector index's actual value entirely, which isn't a form of integrating filtering into ANN search at all.

assessments.prompt: In a RAG pipeline, why must the query be embedded, at request time, using the exact same embedding model that was used to embed and index the source document chunks ahead of time?
options: Using a different model only actually matters if the two models happen to produce vectors of different dimensionality.
It's a stylistic convention rather than a hard requirement -- any reasonably capable modern embedding model would work interchangeably with any other.

Different embedding models produce independent, uncalibrated vector spaces, so comparing a query vector from one model against document vectors from another would yield similarity scores with no real meaning, silently corrupting retrieval without raising any error.
The embedding model choice only affects the quality of the LLM's generated answer, not the retrieval step that happens before it.
assessments.explanation: This is the 'don't mix embedding model versions' rule from the first concept, now a hard requirement for RAG: since two embedding models carve out unrelated, uncalibrated vector spaces, a similarity score computed between a query vector from one model and document vectors from another doesn't correspond to any real relationship. It still returns a number, with no error or warning, but the number is meaningless, so retrieval is bad or irrelevant with nothing signaling it. The “It's a stylistic convention rather…” option is the mistake this rule exists to prevent. The “Using a different model only actually matters…” option is wrong: matching dimensionality is coincidental and doesn't fix the underlying incompatibility between two independently-trained vector spaces. The “The embedding model choice only affects…” option is wrong because this is fundamentally a retrieval-stage problem -- the wrong or irrelevant chunks get retrieved before generation ever happens, which is the kind of retrieval bug the explanation warns gets mistaken for a generation failure.

assessments.prompt: A RAG-powered support chatbot occasionally gives a confident, plausible-sounding, but factually wrong answer, and a teammate suggests the fix is to try a different LLM or add stricter prompt instructions. Explain why you'd want to investigate retrieval first, and what specifically you'd check.
assessments.modelAnswer: Before assuming the generation step is at fault, remember that the LLM can't know whether the context it was handed is relevant. It's given whatever the retrieval step produced and asked to answer from it, and a capable model will confidently synthesize a plausible answer from irrelevant or wrong context as readily as from good context. So a retrieval failure and a genuine generation failure can look identical from the outside: a confident, wrong answer either way. A large share of real RAG failures turn out to be retrieval bugs, and several checkable causes from earlier in this subject produce exactly this symptom: the query might have been embedded with a different model version than the one that built the index (similarity scores that are meaningless rather than merely low), the ANN index's recall might be tuned too low to retrieve the one chunk containing the answer, or a metadata filtering bug might be leaking in irrelevant or wrong-scope content. The first step is to log and inspect the chunks retrieved for the failing query. If that context doesn't contain the information needed to answer correctly, that's conclusive: the model did about as well as it could with what it was given, and the fix belongs in retrieval (checking embedding model consistency, raising recall, auditing filters), not in swapping models or tightening prompt wording, which treats the symptom rather than the upstream cause.
